demo_mom.summary: Your mom is a caring, warm elder who puts family first. She's had a lot on her plate at home lately. She's both worried about Dad's health and full of expectations about your love life. You two are close, but she feels a bit let down when you always say "I'll try" or "we'll see." What you should pay attention to lately is giving her clear answers and not leaving her waiting.

points.text: Caring and action-oriented. She's willing to take on all the family matters herself.
Warm and easily happy. She reacts very directly to big and small good news in the family.
She talks tough and gets a little smug, but deep down she still cares about you.
She cares more about promises and certainty and doesn't like vague answers.
Dad's health, especially his blood pressure, taking his medicine, and quitting alcohol.
You coming home often and settling things down, instead of always saying "we'll see."
Your relationship progress. She wants to meet Amy and add her on WeChat.
For her birthday she doesn't want anything special, just you coming home for a meal.
She's afraid you'll get taken advantage of in love, so she forwards you articles as reminders.
You're close. She sends you things on her own and knits scarves, and you buy food to bring back too.
You're willing to cover Dad's medication costs and go with him to follow-up visits. She declines verbally but is happy inside.
She gets disappointed by your vague answers, but she won't make a big fuss, just complain a little.
She's very attentive to your matters, but she also respects your pace, like telling you not to rush and to take it slow.
When you promise something, try to give a clear time—don't brush it off with "I'll try" or "we'll see later."
Ask a bit more about how her dad's health is doing—she'll feel you care.
Take the initiative to give Amy a rough plan—don't leave her waiting for an answer.
Going home for a meal on her birthday matters a lot to her—try not to reschedule.
When she forwards articles or nags, don't argue about who's right—just go along with a word or two.

demo_sister.summary: Tina is a caring, practical, family-oriented person who habitually takes on everything big and small at home. She both looks after you and has expectations of you. You two are close—she's willing to spend money and effort for you and Mom and Dad, but she'll also push you to shoulder what you should. What to watch lately: don't let her feel that the things she pushes you on always go nowhere, and also check in on her health.

points.text: She's proactive and loves to organize—family matters are often started, fronted, and arranged by her first.
She's generous with family, willing to pay more herself, and even tells you to keep your salary for yourself.
She pushes hard verbally, but if you say "stop interrogating me," she can rein it in—she's not out to pressure you.
She's busy with work, often stays up late, and her body is already sending warnings, but she won't budge on lifestyle habits—like being anemic yet unable to give up coffee.
She cares about Mom and Dad's health and the whole family getting along, and is willing to spend money and effort arranging a massage chair, dehumidifier, and a Sanya trip.
She cares about Momo's company—feels bad when overtime means not being with the kid—and is happy to let Momo help host you.
She cares whether things between you and Amy are seriously moving forward, repeatedly urging you to "settle it"—she's not just saying it.
She cares whether the things you promised have follow-through and will remind you "don't forget again."
You two are close—she'll ask you to go back to Beijing together, remind you to bring warm clothes, and Momo is looking forward to your visit too.
She both looks after you and has expectations: she won't quibble with you over money, but on matters she hopes you're reliable and don't drag things out.
You sometimes drag things out or only agree verbally, so she keeps pushing—and the more she pushes, the more resistant you get.
For things she's asked about, even if nothing's settled, proactively reply with an update—don't make her chase you.
Her body is already sending warnings—you can show some care, like reminding her not to just power through her anemia on coffee.
She fronted money for the trip—be proactive when settling up afterward, don't make her bring it up.
She specifically reminded you about the week of the 17th—confirm clearly before going, don't wait until the last minute to ask.

demo_laoxu.summary: Leo is a loyal guy who shoulders responsibility. Right now he's squeezed by the mortgage, the kid, and bank targets—occasionally anxious and sleepless, but still working hard to find a side hustle. You two are tight—he treats you like one of his own, and the 100-day banquet is a big deal to him lately. You agreed to go and helped out, and he remembers. Going forward, don't let him feel you're brushing him off—especially about drinking and the side hustle—listen more, advise less.

points.text: He values relationships and face, is generous with friends, insists on treating, and loves organizing gatherings.
He knows his limits—when he found the partnership accounts weren't clear, he pulled out in time instead of forcing it.
He agrees quickly but tends to drag on action—like quitting drinking was only verbal, and he never sent you the plan.
He holds things in and mulls them over—when anxious he gets insomnia and self-doubt.
He feels guilty toward family and will be the first to back down and comfort his wife after a fight.
He cares a lot about his son and family—booking the 100-day banquet at Laomendong and telling you to dress well and not be late means he's treating it as a big deal.
He's stressed about money—mortgage over seven thousand, doesn't dare change homes or jobs, and the side hustle is to earn more.
He values friendship—repeatedly reminds you to come to the 100-day banquet and even remembers your "we'll see."
He cares whether he's "not supposed to be trying"—he needs someone to affirm his choices.
You're old friends who can lean on each other—he treats you to meals and takes you fishing, you help him fix the logo and push resources.
He treats you as someone to confide in—after drinking he talks about high school, the mortgage, the kid, and the bank—that's trust.
You helped crucially with his side hustle—logo finalized, mini-program launched—and he recognizes that.
He's a bit worried you'll flake—he reminded you specifically about the fishing trip, and this time he remembered "we'll see."
Don't be late to the 100-day banquet and dress formally—he specifically said so; it's about giving him face.
Don't push hard about drinking—he agrees verbally but it's hard to change; try another way, like inviting him fishing instead of a drinking session.
Affirm his decision to "do it small on his own" with the side hustle—don't pour cold water; he needs that right now.
He invited you to come to Nanjing early for a drink and you replied "we'll see"—better give him a definite answer; he remembers that.
Things like his brother asking for money and the exhaustion of childcare at home—just listen, don't make decisions for him.

demo_azhe.summary: Jason is a young guy grinding at a big company in Hangzhou—recently moved and started a new job, while busy preparing for his wedding. Money is tight and pressure is high, but he trusts you a lot—borrowing money, treating, wedding arrangements all go to you. You two are tight—he treats you as his best man and someone to confide in. What to watch lately: he's under financial pressure and sleeping poorly—don't push him to repay before the wedding, and give him more emotional support.

points.text: He's proud and used to shouldering pressure alone—rarely complains proactively, but occasionally lets his exhaustion show.
He's attentive to friends—repeatedly confirms plans and is willing to treat and pay for the venue.
He knows his limits—when borrowing he proactively proposes a repayment plan, and gives advance notice if he can't pay.
He tends to share good news but not bad—words come to his lips and he swallows them, maybe afraid of burdening others.
He's practical, not into showiness—picked a simple, inexpensive engagement ring and respects his girlfriend's dislike of crowds.
He's very conscious of his finances—moving, wedding, and gift money all pile up, and money worries keep him up at night.
He cares about job stability and income—though he wants to switch jobs, he decided to wait for the year-end bonus and not quit without a plan, and not move before the wedding.
He cares about the wedding flow and how he'll come across—so nervous he sleeps badly, afraid he won't know what to say on stage.
He values friendship—repeatedly reminds you not to flake on ball games and gaming sessions, and proactively invites you to meals.
He wants to fit into the new environment—meeting neighbors and a guy who can refer him through playing ball.
He treats you as a very trusted friend—borrowing money, revising his resume, wedding help all go to you, and he made you his best man.
You share a love of sports—playing ball and gaming together are common ways you interact.
He owes you money but has been paying—some remains, and he says he'll pay after payday.
At the wedding he relies on you to watch the flow, block drinks, and hold the rings—shows he's very at ease with you.
Don't push too hard about the money—he proactively proposed a repayment plan and will pay after payday; pushing only adds to his anxiety.
Give him more emotional support before the wedding—he's nervous about the flow, so proactively ask what he needs help with to put him at ease.
When words come to his lips and he swallows them, don't press—give him space; he'll say it when he's ready.
Try not to flake on agreed ball games and gaming sessions—he cares a lot about that.
He's under work pressure and sleeping poorly—you can casually remind him to rest when chatting, but don't nag.

demo_xiaoyu.summary: Amy is a nurse who works hard but is under a lot of pressure. She's strong-willed and sensitive, and she really cares about your company and your promises. Your relationship is stable and you've reached the meeting-the-parents stage. Lately she's juggling studying for the nurse exam, looking for a place, and not feeling well. What she needs most is for you to talk less and follow through more, and to give her space before the exam.

points.text: She's serious and responsible at work, can hold it together in emergencies, but afterward she gets scared and feels guilty.
Strong-willed, used to carrying things on her own, doesn't like to trouble others, but deep down she wants to be seen and cared for.
Her emotions come out directly—she'll say when she's unhappy, but she gets over it fast and comes around if you give her an out.
She takes promises seriously. If you don't do what you said, she'll be disappointed, maybe even cry.
A little jealous—seeing a photo of you with a female coworker makes her uncomfortable, but she'll say it's not that she doesn't trust you.
Conservative in front of her parents—she keeps the relationship hidden at first and only reveals it slowly once she's sure.
She cares whether you actually do what you promised, especially small concrete things like picking her up, fixing her computer, or developing photos.
She cares about having someone to talk to during night shifts—no red packets, just a few messages.
She cares whether you ask if she's tired after a night shift and whether you feel for her.
She cares about the title/nurse exam—she's under a lot of pressure, afraid she'll fail, and wants less disturbance before the exam.
She cares about living close to the hospital and somewhere quiet. Her roommate bringing her boyfriend home annoys her, and she wants to move ASAP.
She cares how you act when you meet her parents—afraid her mom will find fault with you, and afraid you'll say the wrong thing.
Her eating habits are fixed: no cilantro, milk tea with less sugar and no ice, no cilantro in hotpot.
The relationship is stable and you've reached the meeting-the-parents stage. Her mom knows about you and wants to meet you.
She feels grounded when she's with you, and she's willing to cook for you and give you a cup—signs she's invested in this relationship.
You had one clear trust issue: you overslept and didn't pick her up. She waited forty minutes and said she was disappointed and wanted to cry.
She's already planning to take you back to Hangzhou for her cousin's wedding and to meet her parents—the relationship is heading somewhere more official.
Before the exam she clearly wants fewer dates—not because she doesn't want to see you, but because she needs to focus. She'll make it up to you after.
Put the things you promise her on your calendar and set alarms, especially the small things she keeps bringing up like picking her up after work, fixing her computer, and developing photos.
When she's on night shift or sick, skip the "drink more hot water" and just ask if she's tired, offer to bring congee or milk tea, or chat with her a bit.
During the pre-exam period, cut back on invitations and messages on your own, but check in around mealtimes—don't disappear completely.
Prepare seriously before meeting her parents: bring cherries or tea, not too expensive, dress decently, and don't stammer through your introduction.
When she complains about her roommate or the stress of apartment hunting, help her screen listings and go look at places with her—that's more useful than giving advice.
When she's jealous, don't over-explain—just say you'll keep your distance and reassure her.
If her cooking is too salty you can say so, but add "I could still eat more" so she doesn't feel bad.
